The Current State of Subjective Training
Load Monitoring—a Practical Perspective
and Call to Action
Joseph O. C. Coyne1*, G. Gregory Haff1, Aaron J. Coutts2, Robert U. Newton1 and Sophia Nimphius1


  Abstract
  This commentary delivers a practical perspective on the current state of subjective training load (TL) monitoring,
  and in particular sessional ratings of perceived exertion, for performance enhancement and injury prevention.
  Subjective measures may be able to reflect mental fatigue, effort, stress, and motivation. These factors appear to be
  important moderators of the relationship TL has with performance and injury, and they also seem to differ between
  open and closed skill sports. As such, mental factors may affect the interaction between TL, performance, and injury
  in different sports. Further, modeling these interactions may be limited due to the assumption that an independent
  signal can adequately account for the performance or injury outcomes. An independent signal model does not
  accurately reflect training environments where multiple stressors (e.g., mechanical, emotional, nutritional) impact
  adaptations. Common issues with using subjective TL monitoring, including a lack of differentiation between
  biomechanical, physiological, and cognitive load, may be overcome by considering psychometric measurement
  best practices, finer graded scales, and differential ratings of perceived exertion. Methods of calculating TL,
  including different acute and chronic time periods, may also need to be individualized to different sports and
  potentially different individuals within the same sport. As TL monitoring is predominately a “chronic” decision-
  making tool, “acute” decision-making tools, e.g., subjective wellness and autonomic nervous system measures,
  should be combined in a bespoke multivariate model to aid sports coaches. A call to action is presented for future
  research on key issues associated with TL monitoring that will have relevance for practitioners in an applied setting.

  "practicalImplications": "Coaches should use heart rate-based high-intensity training load when aiming to improve aerobic capacity, and should be cautious about using session RPE, external load or common training impulse models to predict performance changes in team sports.",
  "athleteDev": "For team sport athletes, the review supports monitoring time spent at or above 90% of maximum heart rate to track aerobic development. It gives weak support for using session RPE or external load alone to predict changes in performance.",

{
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in the text, 'The athlete's heart: allometric considerations on published papers and relation to cardiovascular variables', matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Performance", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Endurance Sport", "Swimming & Diving", "Other Sport"],
 "populations": ["Male Athletes", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Pooled analysis of published data from 150 studies (PubMed searched to April 2022, plus reference lists), covering 927 male athletes in skiing, rowing, swimming, cycling, running and weightlifting, and 173 untrained male controls. Left ventricular internal diameter was 7% to 15% larger than in controls, scaled to body weight, in all athletic groups except weightlifters, while wall thickness was 9% to 24% larger in all athletes. Internal diameter correlated with stroke volume, oxygen pulse, maximal oxygen uptake, cardiac output and blood volume (r about 0.9), but wall thickness did not correlate with these variables.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The data come from different studies and populations, mostly cross-sectional and measured at rest, and sport disciplines within a sport were not separated. The correlations are between group means, so they describe the athlete group rather than individual hearts, and they do not show cause.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the scaled heart size differences as individual athlete heart findings or as a reason to flag an athlete, when the paper compares group means from different studies.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2024,
  "citation": "Sejersen C, Volianitis S, Secher NH. The athlete's heart: allometric considerations on published papers and relation to cardiovascular variables. European Journal of Applied Physiology. 2024.",
  "doi": "10.1007/s00421-024-05449-8",
  "abstract": "The authors pooled left ventricular dimensions from published studies of male endurance athletes, weightlifters and untrained controls, scaled to body weight. Left ventricular internal diameter tracked stroke volume, cardiac output and blood volume, while wall thickness did not track these variables.",
  "tldr": "Among male athletes, the enlarged chamber size of the heart is linked to stroke volume and blood volume, while wall thickness is not. Heart size comparisons between sports should be scaled to body weight.",
  "methods": "The authors searched PubMed to April 2022 and added references from prior papers, and included male athletes aged 18 to 40 in endurance sports and weightlifting, with untrained controls. Left ventricular and atrial dimensions and cardiovascular variables were allometrically scaled to body weight and compared with one-way Welch ANOVA, and correlations were tested with Pearson's r. The authors describe the paper as a narrative review, though a search and pooled analysis were carried out.",
  "findings": "The search yielded 150 included studies, with 927 athletes and 173 controls. With scaling to body weight, left ventricular internal diameter was similar in weightlifters and controls and 7% to 15% larger in the other athletic groups, while wall thickness was 9% to 24% larger in all athletes. Internal diameter correlated with stroke volume, oxygen pulse, maximal oxygen uptake, cardiac output and blood volume (r about 0.9), and wall thickness did not correlate with these variables.",
  "limitations": "The heart and exercise data often come from different populations, and the cross-sectional measures at rest may not reflect sport-specific values. Posture and movement artefacts limit exercise measurements, disciplines within a sport were not separated, and scaling used group means rather than individual values. The authors describe the paper as a narrative review, but it also pooled data from a described PubMed search.",
  "practicalImplications": "When comparing heart dimensions across athletes of different body sizes, scale the values to body weight. The evidence supports reading a larger chamber size as linked to blood volume and stroke volume, and a thicker wall as linked to the pressure the heart generates.",
  "athleteDev": "The paper gives context for the expected heart size pattern across endurance sports and weightlifting in male athletes, so coaches and staff can compare athletes within a sport against scaled norms.",
  "rtp": "The paper studies healthy male athletes and does not address injury, cardiac pathology or return to sport. It cannot be used to clear an athlete for return to sport or to judge cardiac risk."
 }
}

{
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in the text, 'The Braking Performance Framework: Practical Recommendations and Guidelines to Enhance Horizontal Deceleration Ability in Multi-Directional Sports', matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Rehabilitation", "Coaching"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport", "Soccer", "American Football", "Basketball", "Rugby"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Practitioner-focused narrative review that proposes a Braking Performance Framework for horizontal deceleration in multi-directional sports, built on the neuromuscular and biomechanical determinants of deceleration. It grades training methods into braking elementary exercises (eccentric yielding, eccentric quasi-isometric and flywheel work) and braking performance exercises (overcoming isometrics, change of direction with a braking step, unanticipated decelerations in small-sided games). The authors give programming tables and state that the evidence for several elements, including heavy assisted braking and dose-response, is limited.",
 "screeningLimitations": "No search method is described, and the framework is an expert synthesis rather than a tested intervention. The authors note that much of the supporting evidence is limited, so the programming guidelines are not validated outcomes.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat the framework's exercise progressions as proven training effects on deceleration, when the authors describe much of the supporting evidence as limited.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2024,
  "citation": "Harper DJ et al. The Braking Performance Framework: Practical Recommendations and Guidelines to Enhance Horizontal Deceleration Ability in Multi-Directional Sports. International Journal of Strength and Conditioning. 2024.",
  "doi": "10.47206/ijsc.v4i1.351",
  "abstract": "The article proposes a Braking Performance Framework to guide the choice of training methods for horizontal deceleration. It sets out exercises built on the known neuromuscular and biomechanical determinants of braking, with practical programming guidelines for practitioners.",
  "tldr": "Horizontal deceleration can be trained with eccentric, isometric, flywheel and change-of-direction exercises, sequenced by the athlete's needs. The authors offer practical programming guidelines drawn from existing evidence, which is limited for several methods.",
  "methods": "Narrative review and practical framework, with no described literature search. The authors draw on the known determinants of horizontal deceleration and on published studies of eccentric, isometric, flywheel and change-of-direction training to propose exercise categories and programming tables.",
  "findings": "The authors propose a framework in which elementary braking exercises build eccentric and isometric capacity, and braking performance exercises apply that capacity to change of direction and unanticipated decelerations in sport. They give programming guidance for flywheel, eccentric yielding, eccentric quasi-isometric and overcoming-isometric work, and note limited research on heavy assisted braking steps and on dose-response.",
  "limitations": "No search method is described, so the selection of evidence cannot be checked. The authors acknowledge that the dose-response relationships and the effects of several exercise types are not well established, so many recommendations are expert judgement.",
  "practicalImplications": "Practitioners can use the framework to choose and progress braking exercises, moving from eccentric and isometric base work toward change-of-direction and unanticipated decelerations in sport. Progressions should be checked against the athlete's response, since dose-response evidence is limited.",
  "athleteDev": "Use the framework to target the eccentric and isometric determinants of deceleration, then progress toward braking in change-of-direction and game-like tasks. Adjust volume and intensity using the athlete's response, because the dose-response evidence is limited.",
  "rtp": "The framework is written for healthy athletes preparing for multi-directional sport, and the authors do not present it as a return-to-sport protocol. Use it for return-to-sport planning only with clinical judgement, because it has not been tested in injured athletes."
 }
}

 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in the text, 'The British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification grading system as a predictor of return to play following hamstrings injury in professional football players', matches the filename (football and soccer are the same sport).",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
 "domains": ["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Rehabilitation", "Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training"],
 "sports": ["Soccer"],
 "populations": ["Male Athletes", "Professional / Elite", "Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Retrospective cohort of 39 primary hamstring strain injuries in male professional players at one English club over 2010 to 2019, where each injury had an MRI within 7 days of onset. Two musculoskeletal radiologists graded the MRIs with the British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC) and with Peetron's system, and the grades were compared with return to play. BAMIC grade correlated weakly with return to play (r = 0.32, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.58, p = 0.05), oedema length correlated weakly and not significantly (r = 0.3, p = 0.06), and cross-sectional area did not correlate (r = 0.02). The two grading systems agreed only slightly (kappa = 0.21).",
 "screeningLimitations": "The sample is 39 injuries from one club, so the confidence intervals are wide and the model explained only 16% of the variance in return to play. The design is retrospective, and the two classifications disagree enough that the grade cannot be read as a precise prediction for an individual player.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read BAMIC as a reliable predictor of an individual player's return date, when the paper reports a weak correlation from a small single-club sample.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2022,
  "citation": "Tears C et al. The British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification grading system as a predictor of return to play following hamstrings injury in professional football players. Physical Therapy in Sport. 2022.",
  "doi": "10.1016/j.ptsp.2022.08.002",
  "abstract": "The authors compared the British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC) grade, oedema length and cross-sectional area on MRI with return to play after primary hamstring strain in 39 professional footballers. BAMIC grade had a weak but significant correlation with return to play, and BAMIC and Peetron's grading agreed only slightly.",
  "tldr": "The BAMIC grade on MRI is weakly linked to how long a professional footballer takes to return to play after a hamstring strain. It agrees only slightly with Peetron's grading, so it should be one input among several.",
  "methods": "Retrospective cohort at one professional English club, 2010 to 2019, with male players who had an MRI within 7 days of a primary hamstring strain. Two musculoskeletal radiologists graded the scans, and Pearson correlations and multiple regression were used to relate the grades and MRI measures to return to play, with kappa for agreement between the two grading systems.",
  "findings": "Among 39 injuries, BAMIC grade correlated weakly with return to play (r = 0.32, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.58, p = 0.05). Oedema length was weakly correlated (r = 0.3, p = 0.06) and cross-sectional area was not (r = 0.02, p = 0.91). The multiple regression explained 16% of the variance in return to play, and kappa for BAMIC against Peetron's was 0.21 (95% CI 0 to 0.42).",
  "limitations": "Only one club was studied, so the sample is small and the regression results are unstable. The authors acknowledge that the lack of significance for cross-sectional area and oedema length may reflect sample size, and call for larger replication. The retrospective design relies on historical MRI and medical records.",
  "practicalImplications": "Grade hamstring strains with BAMIC alongside clinical findings and use the grade as a rough guide to return to play timing. Do not rely on oedema length or cross-sectional area as predictors, and expect weak prediction for individual players.",
  "athleteDev": "Not applicable. The paper studies injured players' return to play after a hamstring strain and does not address performance training.",
  "rtp": "Use BAMIC grading from the first MRI, within 7 days of onset, as one input to return-to-play planning for hamstring strains in professional football. The grade has only weak predictive value, so it should not be used alone to set a return date."
 }
}

 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Methodological / Validation Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains": ["Monitoring & Technology", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Research & Analytics", "Coaching"],
 "sports": ["Basketball"],
 "populations": ["Male Athletes", "Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Observational team case study of 16 semiprofessional male basketball players in a second-tier Australian league, monitored across training sessions in the 2018 season (8 players, face-to-face RPE reporting) and the 2019 season (11 players, phone-based online app). Session RPE was compared with accumulated PlayerLoad and summated heart rate zone workload using repeated-measures correlations. Face-to-face session RPE correlated large with PlayerLoad (r = .69) and very large with summated heart rate zones (r = .74), while the online app correlated small with PlayerLoad (r = .29) and moderate with summated heart rate zones (r = .34), and all correlations were significant.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The two reporting methods were used in different seasons with partly different players (only 3 players overlapped), so method and season are confounded. Reporting windows also differed (30 minutes face-to-face, 60 minutes online), and the study has only 16 players from one team.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the weaker online correlations as proof that any app-based RPE is invalid, when the study compared one team across two seasons with different reporting windows.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2020,
  "citation": "Fox JL, O'Grady CJ, Scanlan AT. The Concurrent Validity of Session-Rating of Perceived Exertion Workload Obtained Face-to-Face Versus Via an Online Application: A Team Case Study. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2020.",
  "doi": "10.1123/ijspp.2019-0908",
  "abstract": "The authors compared session RPE collected face-to-face in one season with session RPE collected by a phone-based online app in another season, in 16 semiprofessional male basketball players. Face-to-face ratings correlated more strongly with PlayerLoad and summated heart rate zone workload than the app ratings did.",
  "tldr": "In this one team, session RPE collected face-to-face tracked objective workload more closely than session RPE collected through a phone app. Basketball staff should check any app-based RPE against objective load before relying on it.",
  "methods": "Observational team case study across the 2018 and 2019 seasons. Players rated session RPE after each session, either face-to-face (2018) or through a phone-based app (2019), and workload was measured by microsensor PlayerLoad and summated heart rate zones. Repeated-measures correlations with 95% confidence intervals were used to compare the two reporting methods.",
  "findings": "All correlations were significant. Face-to-face session RPE correlated large with PlayerLoad (r = .69, 95% CI .07) and very large with summated heart rate zone workload (r = .74). The online app correlated small with PlayerLoad (r = .29) and moderate with summated heart rate zone workload (r = .34).",
  "limitations": "The two methods were compared in different seasons with partly different players, so season and method cannot be separated. Ratings were collected within 30 minutes (face-to-face) and within 60 minutes (online), the sample is 16 players from one team, and the authors describe the design as observational.",
  "practicalImplications": "Collect session RPE face-to-face or within a short, consistent window, and do not assume app-based RPE has the same validity. Check any app-based RPE against objective workload before using it to guide training.",
  "athleteDev": "For basketball training load monitoring, the results favour collecting session RPE individually and soon after training. App-based RPE should be checked against PlayerLoad or heart rate zone workload before it guides load decisions.",
  "rtp": "The study is about training load monitoring in healthy players and does not address injury or return to sport. It cannot be used to set return-to-play loads."
 }
}

{
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in the text, 'The Correlations Between Training Load Parameters and Physical Performance Adaptations in Team Sports: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis', matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance", "Monitoring & Technology"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport", "Soccer", "Rugby", "Basketball", "Other Sport"],
 "populations": ["Male Athletes", "Female Athletes", "Professional / Elite", "Youth / Adolescent"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review and meta-analysis of 40 studies with 726 men and women team sport players, searched in PubMed, Scopus, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science, with an updated search in September 2025. Heart rate-based training impulse correlated with changes in maximal oxygen uptake (r = 0.63), velocity at 2 mmol/L blood lactate (r = 0.47) and velocity at the onset of blood lactate accumulation (r = 0.43). Session RPE correlated with changes in velocity at 2 mmol/L lactate (r = 0.29), and external load measures showed weak associations with strength, power and speed.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The GRADE certainty for every analysis was judged very low, mainly because of risk of bias and imprecision, and the studies were heterogeneous in sport, sex, level and load measures. Most studies were mainly soccer, and the included players are mostly outdoor team sport players, so the pooled correlations may not generalize to other sports.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the pooled correlations as a prescription that heart rate training impulse will produce a given VO2max gain, when the authors rate the evidence as very low certainty.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2025,
  "citation": "Clemente FM et al. The Correlations Between Training Load Parameters and Physical Performance Adaptations in Team Sports: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine - Open. 2025;11:156.",
  "doi": "10.1186/s40798-025-00952-4",
  "abstract": "The authors searched four databases for team sport studies with at least two weeks of training load and pre and post performance tests. Of 40 studies with 726 players, heart rate-based training impulse correlated moderately with endurance adaptations, and session RPE and external load showed limited associations with performance adaptations.",
  "tldr": "In team sport players, heart rate-based training impulse is the training load measure most closely linked to endurance gains. Session RPE and external load show weak links to performance adaptations, and the evidence is of very low certainty.",
  "methods": "Systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA 2020, searching PubMed, Scopus, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science, with an updated search in September 2025. Eligible studies included men or women in team sports at trained or developmental level with at least two weeks of training load and pre and post physical testing. Pooled correlations used random effects, study quality used the Downs and Black scale, and certainty used GRADE.",
  "findings": "Forty studies with 726 players were included. Heart rate-based training impulse correlated with changes in maximal oxygen uptake (r = 0.63), velocity at 2 mmol/L lactate (r = 0.47) and velocity at onset of blood lactate accumulation (r = 0.43). Session RPE correlated with changes in velocity at 2 mmol/L lactate (r = 0.29), and external load measures had weak or no clear associations with strength, power and speed. All analyses were rated very low certainty under GRADE.",
  "limitations": "The authors note uneven coverage of the literature, with most studies in outdoor sports such as soccer and rugby, and few in indoor sports, women or youth. Study quality, heterogeneity and imprecision were all concerns, and the authors note that many analyses were below the sample size needed for precise estimates.",
  "practicalImplications": "Use heart rate-based training impulse when tracking endurance adaptations in team sport players. Do not rely on session RPE or external load alone to predict strength, power or speed gains, and treat the pooled correlations as a guide rather than a prescription.",
  "athleteDev": "For team sport players, heart rate-based training impulse is the most consistent training load signal for endurance development, such as VO2max and lactate thresholds. Strength, power and speed should be tracked with direct testing, since external and session load show weak links to them.",
  "rtp": "The review covers healthy team sport players and does not address injury or return to sport. It cannot be used to set return-to-play loads."
 }
}

 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in the text, 'The Braking Performance Framework: Practical Recommendations and Guidelines to Enhance Horizontal Deceleration Ability in Multi-Directional Sports', matches the filename.",

 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Rehabilitation", "Coaching"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport", "Soccer", "American Football"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Practitioner-focused narrative review that proposes a Braking Performance Framework for horizontal deceleration in multi-directional sports, built on the neuromuscular and biomechanical determinants of deceleration. It grades training methods into braking elementary exercises (eccentric yielding, eccentric quasi-isometric and flywheel work) and braking performance exercises (overcoming isometrics, change of direction with a braking step, unanticipated decelerations in small-sided games). The authors give programming tables and state that the evidence for several elements, including heavy assisted braking and dose-response, is limited.",
 "screeningLimitations": "No search method is described, and the framework is an expert synthesis rather than a tested intervention. The authors note that much of the supporting evidence is limited, so the programming guidelines are not validated outcomes.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat the framework's exercise progressions as proven training effects on deceleration, when the authors describe much of the supporting evidence as limited.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2024,
  "citation": "Harper DJ et al. The Braking Performance Framework: Practical Recommendations and Guidelines to Enhance Horizontal Deceleration Ability in Multi-Directional Sports. International Journal of Strength and Conditioning. 2024.",
  "doi": "10.47206/ijsc.v4i1.351",
  "abstract": "The article proposes a Braking Performance Framework to guide the choice of training methods for horizontal deceleration. It sets out exercises built on the known neuromuscular and biomechanical determinants of braking, with practical programming guidelines for practitioners.",
  "tldr": "Horizontal deceleration can be trained with eccentric, isometric, flywheel and change-of-direction exercises, sequenced by the athlete's needs. The authors offer practical programming guidelines drawn from existing evidence, which is limited for several methods.",
  "methods": "Narrative review and practical framework, with no described literature search. The authors draw on the known determinants of horizontal deceleration and on published studies of eccentric, isometric, flywheel and change-of-direction training to propose exercise categories and programming tables.",
  "findings": "The authors propose a framework in which elementary braking exercises build eccentric and isometric capacity, and braking performance exercises apply that capacity to change of direction and unanticipated decelerations in sport. They give programming guidance for flywheel, eccentric yielding, eccentric quasi-isometric and overcoming-isometric work, and note limited research on heavy assisted braking steps and on dose-response.",
  "limitations": "No search method is described, so the selection of evidence cannot be checked. The authors acknowledge that the dose-response relationships and the effects of several exercise types are not well established, so many recommendations are expert judgement.",
  "practicalImplications": "Practitioners can use the framework to choose and progress braking exercises, moving from eccentric and isometric base work toward change-of-direction and unanticipated decelerations in sport. Progressions should be checked against the athlete's response, since dose-response evidence is limited.",
  "athleteDev": "Use the framework to target the eccentric and isometric determinants of deceleration, then progress toward braking in change-of-direction and game-like tasks. Adjust volume and intensity using the athlete's response, because the dose-response evidence is limited.",
  "rtp": "The framework is written for healthy athletes preparing for multi-directional sport, and the authors do not present it as a return-to-sport protocol. Use it for return-to-sport planning only with clinical judgement, because it has not been tested in injured athletes."
 }
}

  "findings": "Among 39 injuries, BAMIC grade correlated weakly with return to play (r = 0.32, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.58, p = 0.05). Oedema length was weakly correlated (r = 0.3, p = 0.06) and cross-sectional area was not (r = 0.02, p = 0.91).
